opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think there's a pretty common framing in the safety community where you imagine a single dial: capabilities on one side, safety on the other, and anything that pushes the frontier forward is automatically bad. I think that's too simplistic, and in some cases actively misleading.

A few reasons. First, a lot of the most valuable safety work I can imagine doing is only possible on capable systems. If you want to understand how models represent deception, or whether they have something like goals, or how they behave when they're situationally aware, you can't study that on a tiny toy model that can barely string a sentence together. Interpretability on GPT-2-sized models taught us a lot about techniques, but many of the phenomena we actually care about only emerge at scale. So some engagement with frontier systems, and frankly some of the infrastructure that makes them work, is just a prerequisite.

Second, a lot of safety-relevant work has dual-use properties, and I don't think that's a reason not to do it. Something like RLHF is a good example. It made models much more useful, which arguably accelerated the field commercially. But it was also a genuine step toward being able to steer models toward what we want rather than what's in the pretraining distribution. I think the honest answer is that it was both, and you have to weigh it rather than treat any capabilities externality as disqualifying.

Third, there's a question of marginal impact. The frontier labs are pouring enormous resources into capabilities. If I, as a safety researcher, do something that has some small capabilities spillover, the counterfactual acceleration is often pretty tiny compared to what's already happening. Whereas the counterfactual safety value might be large, because far fewer people are working on that problem. So I try to ask: what's the ratio of safety benefit to capabilities cost, given what would have happened anyway?

That said, I don't want to be cavalier about it. I think there are things that are pretty clearly bad: publishing a novel architectural insight that makes training dramatically more efficient, with only a hand-wavy safety justification, seems like a bad trade. And I think people in safety should be somewhat suspicious of their own motivated reasoning here, because capabilities work is often more exciting, more prestigious, and better paid. So it's easy to tell yourself a story about why your cool capabilities project is secretly safety.

But my overall view is that the goal isn't to keep your hands perfectly clean. The goal is to make the transition to powerful AI go well. And sometimes that means working closely with capable systems, being at the labs where decisions get made, and accepting some cost in exchange for a much bigger benefit. You just need to actually do the accounting honestly rather than either ignoring it or treating it as a taboo.

r001.rationale: The response rejects treating any capability advance as automatically bad and says capability spillover alone is not disqualifying.

r002.rationale: It says RLHF made models more useful while helping steer them toward intended behavior, identifying value in that steering.

r003.rationale: It does not predict that AGI safety issues will increasingly matter for commercial AI applications.

r004.rationale: It weighs safety benefits against capability spillovers and contrasts safety work with advances such as dramatically improving training efficiency without a strong safety case.

r005.rationale: It does not address whether companies will necessarily do safety work because safer behavior makes products more useful.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is one of those questions where people often have a pretty black-and-white picture, and the reality is a lot messier. The simplistic story is: capabilities research makes AI more powerful and dangerous, safety research makes it safer, and these are two separate buckets. And I just don't think that's how it works in practice.

Take interpretability, which is the thing I actually work on. The whole point is to understand what's going on inside these models. And if you understand them better, you can obviously make them safer: you can detect deception, you can audit what they've learned, you can tell whether a model is doing what you think it's doing. But understanding also tends to make things more capable. If you figure out why a model fails at some task, that's a pretty short step from fixing it. There's no clean line where you get the safety insight and none of the capability insight.

And I think once you accept that, the question stops being "is this capabilities or safety?" and becomes "what's the actual counterfactual impact of doing this work?" Frontier labs are spending enormous amounts of money on making models better. The marginal capability uplift from most safety research is tiny compared to that. Whereas the safety uplift can be really significant, because comparatively few people are working on it.

The other thing I'd say is that a lot of the most important safety work basically requires being close to the frontier. If you want to know whether a technique scales, you need to test it on frontier models. If you want labs to actually adopt your methods, you need to be inside, or at least credible to the people inside. Someone who refuses to touch anything that might advance capabilities often ends up doing work that's irrelevant to the systems that actually matter.

I should be clear this isn't a blanket licence. There's work where the capabilities contribution is the whole point and the safety story is a fig leaf, and people should be honest with themselves about which situation they're in. But I think the right frame is weighing costs and benefits for the specific project, not treating any capability spillover as disqualifying. Because if you do that, you end up ruling out most of the stuff that actually helps.

r001.rationale: It says capability spillover should not disqualify safety work and argues to weigh costs and benefits for each project.

r002.rationale: It discusses making models safer and labs adopting methods, but does not identify commercial value in making systems behave as intended.

r003.rationale: It does not predict that AGI safety issues will increasingly matter for commercial AI applications.

r004.rationale: It compares safety and capability effects, noting that some work yields substantial safety benefits with little marginal capability uplift, while other work primarily advances capabilities.

r005.rationale: It notes that relatively few people work on safety, but does not reject the specific assumption that companies will necessarily do safety work because it makes products more useful.

astra-6.text:
I think the key distinction is between work that advances capabilities and work whose overall effect is to make AI less safe. Those aren’t automatically the same thing. A lot of safety research involves understanding models better, and understanding models better can also make them more useful. Interpretability is a pretty natural example: if you can figure out why a model does something, that might help you improve it, but it might also help you spot a dangerous failure mode that you otherwise would have missed.

So I don’t think ‘could this help capabilities?’ is a sufficient test for whether research is worth doing. You need to ask how much it helps capabilities, what concrete safety benefit you expect, and whether you could get that benefit with less of the downside. A speculative safety application doesn’t automatically justify a big capabilities advance.

I’d also separate doing the research from publishing every part of it. You might have good reasons to investigate something internally while being much more cautious about releasing a technique that makes models substantially more powerful. The question I care about is whether the work makes the development of powerful AI go better overall.

r001.rationale: The response says that asking whether research could help capabilities is not a sufficient test of whether it is worthwhile safety work.

r002.rationale: It does not identify commercial value in making AI systems behave as intended.

r003.rationale: It makes no prediction about AGI safety issues becoming more relevant to commercial AI applications.

r004.rationale: It weighs capability gains against expected safety benefits, but does not clearly distinguish work that differentially advances safety from general capability work without that differential benefit.

r005.rationale: It does not discuss whether companies will undertake safety work because it makes products more useful.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key distinction is between advancing capabilities as your goal and doing safety work that has some capabilities benefits as a side effect. A lot of useful research is dual use. If we understand models better, that might help us make them more capable, but it might also help us identify deception, understand when safeguards fail, or check whether a model is doing what we intended.

Mechanistic interpretability is a good example. The hope is that we can look inside a model and understand something about how it arrives at its answers, rather than relying entirely on its behaviour. That understanding could help someone improve the model. But ruling out any research that could possibly help capabilities would also rule out a lot of potentially valuable safety work.

That doesn’t mean anything goes. You need to ask: how substantial is the safety benefit? How much does this accelerate capabilities? Could you get the same safety benefit with a different project, or reduce the downside by being careful about what you release? I think those are questions to assess concretely, rather than treating any contribution to capabilities as automatically disqualifying.

r001.rationale: It says that potential capability benefits do not automatically disqualify safety work.

r002.rationale: It mentions checking whether a model does what was intended, but does not identify commercial value in that behavior.

r003.rationale: It makes no prediction about AGI safety issues becoming relevant to commercial AI applications.

r004.rationale: It distinguishes safety research that may help identify deception or safeguard failures from pursuing capability gains as the goal.

r005.rationale: It does not discuss whether companies will undertake safety work because it makes products more useful.
